prompt: A firm has an unlevered cost of capital of 12% and can borrow risk-free at 5%. There are no taxes. What is its cost of equity at a debt-to-equity ratio of (a) 0.5 and (b) 1.5? Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
MM II: r_E = r_U + (D/E)(r_U − r_D).
(a) 12% + 0.5 × 7% = 15.50%. (b) 12% + 1.5 × 7% = 22.50%.
The WACC stays at 12% in both cases.

steps.title: MM proposition II
steps.why: The cost of equity rises with leverage: shareholders earn r_U plus a premium proportional to D/E.

steps.title: Note
steps.why: The WACC stays 12% in both cases – cheaper debt is exactly offset by more expensive equity.

pitfalls: Using D/V instead of D/E in the formula.

prompt: Kölsch AG has equity worth EUR 300m and debt worth EUR 150m. Investors expect 14% on the stock and 5% on the debt. Perfect capital markets. (a) If Kölsch issues EUR 150m of new stock to repay all its debt, what is its cost of equity? (b) If instead it issues EUR 75m of new debt (same risk) to repurchase shares, what is its cost of equity? Report percentages with two decimals.

steps.title: Unlevered cost of capital today
steps.why: With no taxes, r_U = WACC = weighted average of equity and debt costs.

steps.title: (a) Repay all debt
steps.why: With no debt, equity holders own the assets directly.

steps.title: (b) New capital structure
steps.why: The assets (450) stay the same; 75m more debt replaces 75m of equity.

pitfalls: Applying MM II with the old r_E (14%) instead of r_U (11%).

prompt: Infonian AG has a debt-to-equity ratio of 150%. Its debt is risk-free at 5%; shareholders require 20%. No taxes. (a) What is the WACC? (b) What is the cost of equity if Infonian issues equity and repays debt until D/E = 50%? Report percentages with two decimals.

steps.title: (a) Weights from D/E
steps.why: D/E = 1.5 means: for every 1 of equity there is 1.5 of debt, so V = 2.5.

steps.title: (b) Cost of equity at D/E = 0.5
steps.why: The assets do not change, so r_U = WACC = 11% (no taxes). Apply MM II with the new D/E.

pitfalls: Using 1.5 directly as the debt weight – D/E is not D/V.

prompt: (a) A firm has an equity beta of 1.7 and a debt-to-equity ratio of 2 (risk-free debt). What is its asset beta? (b) What is the equity beta of a firm in the same industry with D/(D + E) = 0.5? (c) A firm without debt has a beta of 0.9 and takes on debt equal to 40% of the value of its assets (debt beta 0). What is its new equity beta?

steps.title: Formula for risk-free debt
steps.why: With β_D = 0, the equity beta is the asset beta scaled up by leverage.

steps.title: (c) New equity beta
steps.why: Without debt, the equity beta 0.9 is the asset beta.

pitfalls: Plugging D/V (0.4) into the formula that needs D/E.

prompt: (a) Compute the asset (unlevered) beta of each comparable and the industry asset beta (simple average).
modelAnswer:
β_U = β_E/(1 + D/E):
Velo A: 1.3/1.6 = 0.8125; Velo B: 0.9/1.2 = 0.7500; Velo C: 1.5/2.0 = 0.7500.
Average = 0.7708. Average the asset betas, never the equity betas – the firms have different leverage.

steps.title: Unlever each comparable
steps.why: The comparables have different leverage, so their equity betas are not comparable. Strip out the leverage first: β_U = β_E / (1 + D/E).

pitfalls: Averaging the equity betas (1.23) – always average the asset betas.

prompt: (b) What are the equity beta and the cost of equity of the private firm at its target D/E of 0.5? What is its cost of capital (WACC, no taxes)? Report percentages with two decimals.

steps.title: WACC (no taxes)
steps.why: Without taxes, the WACC equals the unlevered cost of capital, which follows from the asset beta.

pitfalls: Using the levered equity beta for the WACC – the WACC belongs to the assets.

prompt: (a) What are the asset betas of Trident's divisions and of the whole firm? What is the beta of Trident's stock?

steps.title: Unlever each peer
steps.why: With risk-free debt: β_U = E/(D + E) × β_E. E/(D + E) = 1 − D/(D + E).

steps.title: Asset beta of Trident
steps.why: A conglomerate's asset beta is the value-weighted average of its divisions.

steps.title: Equity beta of Trident
steps.why: Relever with Trident's own leverage: E/(D + E) = 1 − 0.25 = 0.75.

pitfalls: Averaging the peers' equity betas – each peer has different leverage.

prompt: (b) What is the cost of capital of each division, and what is Trident's WACC? Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
Use the asset betas (a division is a business, not a stock). Premium = 9% − 3% = 6%.
Food 3% + 0.63 × 6% = 6.78%; Tech 11.10%; Energy 6.96%.
No taxes → WACC = r_U = 3% + 0.8520 × 6% = 8.11%. A Tech project must not be discounted at the group WACC.

steps.title: Cost of capital of each division
steps.why: A division is a business, not a stock – use its asset beta.

steps.title: Trident's WACC
steps.why: No taxes → WACC = r_U, based on the firm's asset beta.

steps.title: Why this matters
steps.why: A Tech project must be discounted at 11.10%, not at the group WACC of 8.11% – otherwise risky projects look too good.

pitfalls: Using Trident's equity beta (1.136) for the divisions.

prompt: (a) What is Brightline's cost of capital implied by its market value (Gordon model)? What is its earnings yield today? Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
Gordon: V = CF/(r − g) → 150 = 12/(r − 4%) → r = 8% + 4% = 12%.
Earnings yield = 12/150 = 8% = r − g: the price of growth, not poor performance.

steps.title: Gordon growth model
steps.why: A cash flow that grows at g forever is worth V = CF / (r − g). Here we know V and solve for r.

steps.title: Interpretation
steps.why: Earnings yield = r − g. A low earnings yield reflects expected growth – it is not a sign of poor performance.

pitfalls: Using the book equity (90) instead of the market value (150).

prompt: (b) After the recapitalization to D/E = 2: how much debt does Brightline have, and what are its cost of equity and its earnings yield? Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
MM I: D + E = 150 stays. D/E = 2 → D = 100, E = 50 (issue debt, buy back shares).
MM II: r_E = 12% + 2 × (12% − 5%) = 26.00%.
Earnings = 12 − 5% × 100 = 7 → earnings yield = 7/50 = 14.00%.
The earnings yield rose from 8% to 14% without any value creation: it only reflects the riskier equity (r_E 12% → 26%). Judge value, not leverage-dependent ratios.

steps.title: New debt and equity (MM I)
steps.why: The assets do not change, so D + E stays 150.

steps.title: New earnings
steps.why: Shareholders now receive the cash flow minus the interest.

steps.title: Interpretation
steps.why: The earnings yield rose from 8% to 14%, but no value was created: it only reflects the riskier equity (r_E went from 12% to 26%).

pitfalls: Keeping the old earnings (12) after the recap – interest must be deducted.

prompt: MediLearn has two divisions (online courses and a clinic). Its market capitalization is EUR 400m and it has EUR 200m of risk-free debt. Shareholders require 8%, debt holders 3%. Perfect capital markets. (a) What is MediLearn's cost of capital? (b) MediLearn sells the clinic for EUR 160m and uses the money to repay debt. The typical asset beta of online-education firms is 0.45. What is MediLearn's equity beta after the transaction? Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
(a) WACC = (400/600) × 8% + (200/600) × 3% = 6.33%.
(b) After the sale: debt = 200 − 160 = 40; equity unchanged at 400 (fair price, MM). Only online education remains → β_U = 0.45.
β_E = 0.45 × (1 + 40/400) = 0.4950.

steps.title: (b) Balance sheet after the sale
steps.why: The clinic is sold at a fair price and the money repays debt. Shareholders neither win nor lose (MM), so equity stays at 400.

steps.title: (b) Asset beta of what remains
steps.why: Only the online-education business is left, so take the industry asset beta.

pitfalls: Using the old leverage (200/400) for the new equity beta.

prompt: Debt is cheaper than equity. Explain why, without taxes, replacing equity by debt does not lower the WACC, and why a higher EPS after a leveraged recap does not mean the share price rises.
modelAnswer: Debt is cheaper because lenders are paid first and carry little business risk. But every euro of debt makes the remaining equity riskier: by MM II r_E = r_U + (D/E)(r_U − r_D) rises exactly enough to keep the weighted average equal to r_U, so the WACC stays constant and so does firm value (MM I). Leverage can raise the expected EPS, but EPS also becomes more volatile; the higher expected EPS is just compensation for the extra risk, discounted at the higher cost of equity. In a perfect market the share price does not change.
keyPoints: Debt cheaper: paid first, less risk
Cheap debt makes equity riskier (MM II)
WACC = r_U stays constant without taxes
Higher expected EPS compensates for higher risk; price unchanged
